title: Willow bicycle basket liner
subtitle: Basketry: a flat-base willow insert for a standard wire bicycle basket
excerpt: A flat-woven willow mat with turned-up sides that fits inside a wire bicycle front basket to line it. The willow liner keeps small items from falling through the wire, improves the look of the basket, and can be lifted out for cleaning. Woven in buff willow using simple randing and a short trac border.
sourceNotes: Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the flat-mat willow construction with turned sides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The simplest willow weaving pattern: a single weaver worked under and over each stake in alternating sequence. The body weave of most baskets.
A simple woven border where each stake is bent and threaded behind the neighbouring stakes to form a neat finished edge.
Willow boiled to fix a tan colour and stripped of bark. The standard material for traditional English willow baskets.
A pointed metal tool for opening gaps in basketry weave to thread new rods.

content.text: A willow bicycle basket liner is a flat-woven mat with short turned-up sides, in structural terms, a very shallow tray. It is an intermediate project because the corners require accurate mitring of the side stakes and the flat base must be tight enough to not flex when loaded. The liner is made to fit a specific basket, so the first step is to measure your wire basket.

Measure your wire basket before cutting any willow: take the internal length, width, and depth. The willow liner should be 1 cm smaller on each dimension to allow for the thickness of the weave and to ensure it sits inside the wire frame rather than sitting on top of it.

: about 20 base sticks (length matching your basket width + 8 cm), 20 side stakes (length = basket width + basket depth × 2 + 10 cm), about 40 weavers for the base and side. Soak overnight, rest in damp cloth 30 minutes before starting.
Lay the base sticks parallel, evenly spaced at 12 mm apart, in a line. Use one thin weaver to start a simple

pass across all the base sticks. Continue randing until the mat reaches the correct length, use the wire basket as a guide, checking the mat against it every few rows. Keep the edges straight by pressing the sticks firmly together at the edges.
Insert the side stakes alongside the base sticks at the long edges of the mat. These stakes will be bent upright to form the sides. Use the
to open the weave alongside each base stick and push the side stake in alongside it. Bend all stakes upright and lock with two waling passes along each long side.

Work the side walls in randing until they reach the basket depth (typically 6, 10 cm). At the short-end corners, the stakes are simply woven in as normal. Work the same height on both long sides before working the trac border.
on all four sides: each stake is bent in front of one stake to the right, behind the next, and out to the front. Complete all the way around. Trim all ends flush.

Dry the liner for 48 hours. Check the fit in the wire basket before it is fully dry, the willow is still flexible enough to adjust if slightly too tight. A liner that fits properly will sit inside the wire frame without being forced, and can be lifted out easily.

attrs.symptom: The base mat curls upward at the edges
attrs.cause: Tension from the weavers is pulling the base sticks inward; the mat is not being held flat during weaving
attrs.fix: Place the mat on a flat surface with a heavy weight in the centre during weaving. Alternatively, peg the base sticks to a flat board with clothes pegs while the first few waving rows set the tension.
